```{r}
#| label: setup
library(pacman)
p_load(tidyverse, tidymodels, here, gt, GGally)
tidymodels_prefer()

# load data
phones <- here("data/smartphone_cleaned_v5.csv") |>
read_csv(show_col_types = FALSE)
```

```{r}
# 1. Data Cleaning
# - remove the 2 luxury editions where their price comes from gold/materials
# - perform transformation, log the price as it is heavily right-skewed
# - recode 5G and NFC to Yes/No so the dummy names are readable
# - keeps the 7 biggest brands, pool the rest into "Other", and make "xiami" the base reference level.
# - keeps only the 12 variables used, then drop incomplete rows.
phones_clean <- phones |>
  filter(!model %in% c("Vertu Signature Touch", 
                       "Xiaomi Redmi K20 Pro Signature Edition")) |>
  mutate(
    log_price = log(price),
    has_5g = factor(if_else(as.logical(has_5g), "Yes", "No"), 
                    levels = c("No", "Yes")),
    has_nfc = factor(if_else(as.logical(has_nfc), "Yes", "No"),
                     levels = c("No", "Yes")),
    brand_group = fct_relevel(fct_lump_n(brand_name, n = 7), "xiaomi")
  ) |>
  select(log_price, processor_speed, ram_capacity, internal_memory, refresh_rate, primary_camera_rear, primary_camera_front, battery_capacity, screen_size, has_5g, has_nfc, brand_group
  ) |>
  na.omit()
```

```{r}
# 2. Split: 75% training, 25% testing
set.seed(41352)
phone_split <- initial_split(phones_clean, prop = 0.75, strata = log_price)
phone_training <- training(phone_split)
phone_test <- testing(phone_split)
```

```{r}
# 3. Recipe: normalise -> PCA on the 6 specifications -> dummy variables -> drop constants
phone_recipe <- recipe(log_price ~ ., data = phone_training) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_pca(processor_speed, ram_capacity, internal_memory, refresh_rate, primary_camera_rear, primary_camera_front, threshold = 0.7, id = "pca") |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_zv(all_predictors())
```

```{r}
# 4. Prep
phone_prep <- prep(phone_recipe)
```

# Data preparation and PCA {background-color="#1F4E79"}

## Are the specifications correlated? {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: corr-numbers
# Numbers used in the text of this slide
pca_vars <- phones_clean |>
  select(processor_speed, ram_capacity, internal_memory, refresh_rate, primary_camera_rear, primary_camera_front)

cor_long <- cor(pca_vars) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column("v1") |>
  pivot_longer(-v1, names_to = "v2", values_to = "r") |>
  filter(v1 < v2)            # keep each pair once

top_pair <- slice_max(cor_long, r, n = 1)
low_pair <- slice_min(cor_long, r, n = 1)
```

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
#| label: fig-corr
#| fig-cap: "Correlations among the six specifications used in the PCA."
#| fig-height: 5
ggcorr(pca_vars, label = TRUE, label_round = 2)
```
:::

:::: {.column width="45%"} 
@fig-corr shows that six specifications are positively correlated. The strongest correlation is between `r top_pair$v1` and `r top_pair$v2` (`r round(top_pair$r, 2)`), and the weakest is between `r low_pair$v1` and `r low_pair$v2` (`r round(low_pair$r, 2)`).

::: fragment
Variables that move together carry overlapping information. Therefore PCA is suitable, because it combines them into fewer uncorrelated components.
:::
:::: 
::::::

::: notes 
The heatmap is the evidence that PCA suits the data. If the variables were unrelated, PCA would not be able to summarise them.
:::

## Data preparation {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: prep-numbers
n_raw   <- nrow(phones)
n_clean <- nrow(phones_clean)
n_miss  <- n_raw - 2 - n_clean
```

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| label: tbl-prep
#| tbl-cap: "Number of smartphones at each preparation step."
tibble(
  step = c(
    "Original dataset",
    "Luxury editions removed",
    "Incomplete records removed",
    "Used in the analysis",
    "Training set (75%)",
    "Testing set (25%)"
  ),
  smartphones = c(n_raw, 2, n_miss, n_clean, nrow(phone_training), nrow(phone_test))
) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(step = "Step", smartphones = "Smartphones")
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"} 
@tbl-prep shows that `r n_clean` of the `r n_raw` smartphones are used.

- Two luxury editions were removed because their prices reflect gold and premium materials rather than specifications.
- Incomplete records were removed because PCA cannot handle missing values.
- Price was logged because it is strongly right-skewed.
:::
:::::

::: notes 
Brand was reduced to the 7 largest brands plus Other, with xiaomi as the comparison group. 5G and NFC were recoded to No and Yes. 
:::

## Method and justification {.smaller}

| Choice | Reason |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| **PCA** on six specifications | The specifications overlap strongly, so using them directly in a regression would cause multicollinearity. PCA replaces them with a few uncorrelated components. |
| **Standardise** before PCA | The variables use different units (GB, GHz, Hz, MP). Without standardising, variables with large numbers would dominate the components. |
| **Linear regression** | The business question is what drives price, and log price is a numeric outcome. |
| **Variables left out** | Rating is almost a copy of the specifications. Fast charging is missing for most iPhone, which would remove most Apple phones. |

::: notes 
Normalise comes before the dummy step so that the 0/1 dummy variables are not rescaled. 
:::

## Preprocessing steps {.smaller}

| Step | What it does | Why |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| 1\. Standardise | Puts all numeric predictors on the same scale | Fair weighting in PCA |
| 2\. PCA | Combines the six specifications into components, keeping enough to explain at least 70% of the variance | Removes overlap, keeps the key information |
| 3\. Dummy variables | Turns 5G, NFC and brand group into 0/1 columns | Regression needs numbers |
| 4\. Remove constants | Drops any column with a single value | Avoids useless predictors |

::: fragment 
The recipe is learned from the training data only and then applied to the testing data. This avoids information leaking from the testing set. 
:::

## Variance explained {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: var-numbers
var_tbl <- tidy(phone_prep, id = "pca", type = "variance")

# number of components kept = number of PC columns after bake()
n_pc <- bake(phone_prep, new_data = NULL) |>
select(starts_with("PC")) |>
ncol()

pc1_var <- var_tbl |>
filter(terms == "percent variance", component == 1) |>
pull(value)

cum_var <- var_tbl |>
filter(terms == "cumulative percent variance", component == n_pc) |>
pull(value)
```

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| label: tbl-var
#| tbl-cap: "Variance explained by each principal component."
var_tbl |>
  filter(terms %in% c("percent variance", "cumulative percent variance")) |>
  mutate(component = paste0("PC", component)) |>
  pivot_wider(id_cols = component, names_from = terms, values_from = value) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(component = "Component",
             `percent variance` = "Variance (%)",
             `cumulative percent variance` = "Cumulative (%)") |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(`percent variance`, `cumulative percent variance`),
             decimals = 1)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| label: fig-scree
#| fig-cap: "Percentage of variance explained by each component."
#| fig-height: 4
var_tbl |>
  filter(terms == "percent variance") |>
  ggplot(aes(component, value)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2C7FB8") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:6) +
  labs(x = "Component", y = "Percentage of variance") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16)
```
:::
:::::

## Number of components retained

@tbl-var and @fig-scree show that PC1 explains `r round(pc1_var, 1)`% of the variance in the six specifications.

::: fragment
The first `r n_pc` components together explain `r round(cum_var, 1)`%. Therefore, `r n_pc` components are retained, which meets the 70% threshold while keeping the components easy to interpret.
:::

::: fragment 
The remaining components add little extra information. The next step is to examine the loadings to describe what each retained component represents.
:::

::: notes 
The 70% threshold is set in step_pca(). R keeps the smallest number of components whose cumulative variance reaches 70%.
:::
